newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Stunned Sandinistas charge Somoza is back.
newsitem.headline: Stunned Sandinistas charge Somoza is back.

text.p: If the apparent victory of right-winger Arnoldo Aleman in Nicaragua's presidential vote dealt a tough political blow to the left-wing Sandinistas, its emotional impact was devastating, activists said on Friday.

Aleman, the burly former mayor of Managua, is known for his fierce anti-Sandinista stance and alleged ties to supporters of former Nicaraguan dictator Anastasio Somoza, who was toppled by the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

Throughout a bitter, polarised election campaign the Sandinistas equated an Aleman victory with a return to the Somoza dictatorship. His apparent triumph, some say, is a stake through the heart of their revolution.
"It's too much to bear. After all these years of revolution and struggle we're going back to Somoza," teary-eyed Sandinista activist Mariana Flores told Reuters.

Adding to the bitterness of Aleman's victory over former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega in Sunday's elections are allegations by party activists and the pro-Sandinista media that the vote was fraudulent.

International observers, including former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, have said the elections were flawed but fair and discount allegations of fraud. With a preliminary vote count 87 percent complete Aleman tops Ortega, 49 to 38 percent.

While Aleman's Liberal Alliance party has already celebrated victory, Ortega has refused to concede defeat, waiting for election officials to doublecheck a vote count he said was riddled with "serious irregularities."

"Could it be possible that after we Nicaraguans defeated the Somoza dictatorship -- at a cost of 50,000 lives -- they return to power, and what is worse, as saviours?" an editorial titled "Humor in the Time of Fraud" in the Sandinista-owned newspaper Barricada asked. "Has half the population plus one gone crazy and become masochists who love the butcher, or is this a nightmare from which we will awake?"
If it is a nightmare it is a vivid one, as the Sandinistas have watched jubilant Aleman supporters dancing to salsa music, chanting "When will the Sandinistas return? -- Never!"

"This election represents a return of the right wing in Nicaragua. This right wing includes former Somoza supporters who will try to come back through the back door," political analyst Oscar Rene Vargas told Reuters.

Many right-wingers fled under the 1979-1990 Marxist government after the state confiscated their property. But the broad support the Sandinistas enjoyed after they toppled the hated Somoza disappeared by the late 1980s as an eight-year civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels left 25,000 dead and failed socialist policies left the economy in ruins.

Analysts say Aleman does have Somoza sympathisers among his backers, mostly in exile in Miami, and while distancing himself from Somoza he has never attacked the former dictator with the same fervor he aims at the Sandinistas.
Aleman denies he belonged to pro-Somoza youth groups before the revolution but has admitted his father and brother had ties to the Somoza government.

Rene Vargas said the election did not spell the end for the Sandinistas, who won a large bloc in the National Assembly and municipal councils and still are the backbone of the army, police and labour unions. But symbolically it was crushing.

Sitting in a park neighbouring party headquarters, Flores swings between anger and sadness. "A lot of militants are angry and would like to protest like we did during the struggle, but times are different now," she said. "I'm trying not to lose my revolutionary ideals, but it's difficult."
